evaluation_plan:
1) Attack implementation and evaluation (synthetic K-armed Bernoulli/Gaussian bandits, K in {5,10,50}, T up to 1e5, gap profiles from easy to hard). Observers see only a_1..a_T. Attacks: (a) Count-argmax; (b) Switch-time MLE for UCB1/KL-UCB/Successive Elimination: given the known algorithm and observed actions, solve for the set of empirical-mean trajectories consistent with 'played arm had the largest index at every round', via a constrained least-squares / interval-propagation estimator on index crossings, outputting a gap estimate; (c) Sequential importance sampling ('particle inversion') for Thompson Sampling and EXP3, where each particle carries a hypothesized reward history reweighted by the probability the algorithm would have chosen the observed action. Metrics vs. round t: best-arm identification accuracy, L2 error of gap estimates, and the *leakage ratio* = attacker error divided by the error of an oracle observer who sees all rewards; also empirical mutual information I(argmax arm ; a_1..t) estimated by Monte Carlo over random instances. Prediction to test: leakage ratio is O(1) for deterministic index algorithms and grows for randomized ones.
2) Leakage audit across algorithms: UCB1, KL-UCB, Successive Elimination, ETC, Thompson Sampling, EXP3, epsilon-greedy, and DP variants (DP-SE, private UCB at eps in {0.1,1,10}). Report 'leakage time' tau_0.9 = first round the best attack reaches 90% best-arm accuracy, alongside regret. Key comparison: DP algorithms should not increase tau_0.9 much, empirically demonstrating that DP does not buy aggregate secrecy.
3) Lower bound validation: instantiate the theoretical bound epsilon-secrecy => regret >= c*eps*Delta*T on 2- and 3-armed instances by grid-searching over parameterized algorithms (mixtures of committed policies) and plotting achieved (regret, attacker error) pairs against the theoretical frontier.
4) Frontier algorithms: implement (i) Decoy-m: run successive elimination but stop eliminating once m candidates remain and thereafter play the survivors with symmetrized counts in a randomly permuted round-robin; (ii) Count-symmetrization wrapper: given any base algorithm, play its recommendation but maintain a randomized 'shadow budget' that forces the play-count vector of the top-m arms to be exchangeable; (iii) Delayed-commit: postpone commitment past a leakage budget. Measure regret vs. best-achievable attacker accuracy, and verify the predicted Pareto shape; compare against the lower bound.
5) Real data: Open Bandit Dataset and MovieLens-1M converted to a K-armed / linear bandit via replay. Run UCB and TS, run the attacks on the action logs, and report attacker accuracy in identifying the top item and in ranking items (Kendall tau vs. true means). Linear-bandit extension: attacker estimates theta direction from the action log of LinUCB; metric = cosine similarity to true theta over time.
6) The dual 'free-riding' experiment: agent B observes only agent A's actions (A runs UCB, B pulls arms in its own copy of the environment and gets rewards but no exploration budget beyond following B's inferred belief). Compare B's regret to (a) running its own UCB, (b) an oracle told the best arm. Also test the adversarial converse: does running a frontier algorithm from (4) measurably slow the free-rider, and at what cost to the leader's own regret?
expected_contribution: Three lines are adjacent but distinct. (1) Differential privacy in bandits (Mishra & Thakurta; Shariff & Sheffet; joint-DP contextual bandits; recent 'Faster Rates for Private Adversarial Bandits') protects an *individual* reward observation from an adversary who sees the action stream; by design it still permits -- indeed guarantees -- learning and hence revealing the *population-level* conclusion (which arm is best, what the gaps are). We study exactly this orthogonal, aggregate leakage, analogous to property/distribution-inference attacks in supervised learning (Ateniese et al.; Suri & Evans) which have never been formulated for sequential decision making. (2) Inverse/structural estimation of decision makers: 'Learning from a Learner' (Jacq et al., 2019) and inverse RL recover rewards from a learning agent's policies, and econometric dynamic-discrete-choice work estimates payoffs from choices; these aim to build an imitator and assume rich access (policies, states, sometimes rewards). We instead treat the action log as a side channel, give algorithm-aware maximum-likelihood attacks that exploit the *deterministic index structure* of UCB/elimination (switch times encode empirical means), and prove attacker-side sample-complexity guarantees plus algorithm-side impossibility results. (3) Adversarial attacks on bandits (reward poisoning, attacks on cooperative multi-agent bandits) and free-riding/communication in multi-agent bandits assume reward or message channels; our observer is strictly weaker (actions only, no rewards, no communication), which makes both the attack and the free-riding result surprising. To our knowledge no prior work defines an information-theoretic secrecy notion for the *identity of the optimal arm*, nor characterizes its price in regret.
motivation_or_abstract: Bandit algorithms are usually analyzed as if their action stream were a private byproduct of learning. In practice the action stream is the most public thing about a deployed system: displayed prices, shown ads, recommended items, and prescribed treatments are all observable, while rewards are not. We ask a simple question: how much does a bandit algorithm reveal to an observer who sees only which arm was pulled at each round? We formalize a passive eavesdropper performing property inference on the action log, with two targets: identifying the optimal arm and estimating the gap vector. First, we show that action logs are startlingly informative. Beyond a naive argmax-of-counts attack, we derive algorithm-aware likelihood attacks that invert the deterministic index dynamics of UCB and successive elimination: the times at which the played arm switches pin down the empirical means, letting an observer estimate gaps at a rate within a constant factor of an observer who saw all the rewards. A sequential Monte Carlo attack extends this to Thompson Sampling and EXP3. Second, we prove this leakage is unavoidable: via a Fano/change-of-measure argument, any algorithm with regret R_T admits an attacker whose best-arm error probability is O(R_T / (Delta T)), so epsilon-secrecy forces linear regret with an explicit constant, yielding a matching regret-secrecy frontier. We then design decoy-set and count-symmetrization wrappers that attain this frontier, and show that DP-bandit algorithms sit far from it. Finally we flip the attack into an algorithm: a second agent that merely watches a UCB agent achieves near-optimal regret with zero exploration cost, making exploration a public good. Experiments on synthetic bandits and real recommendation logs quantify per-algorithm leakage.
problem_statement: The sequence of arms pulled by a bandit algorithm -- with no reward information whatsoever -- is nearly a sufficient statistic for the reward means the algorithm has learned, so any low-regret algorithm necessarily broadcasts its private conclusions to any passive observer; there is a quantifiable Pareto frontier between regret and 'aggregate secrecy' that differential privacy for bandits does not address at all.
proposed_direction: The sequence of arms pulled by a bandit algorithm -- with no reward information whatsoever -- is nearly a sufficient statistic for the reward means the algorithm has learned, so any low-regret algorithm necessarily broadcasts its private conclusions to any passive observer; there is a quantifiable Pareto frontier between regret and 'aggregate secrecy' that differential privacy for bandits does not address at all.
risks_or_caveats: (1) The headline impossibility result may be viewed as intuitive: exploiting the best arm necessarily reveals it. We mitigate this by making the statement quantitative (an explicit constant-level frontier with matching upper and lower bounds) and by focusing the surprise on the *gap-estimation* attack, where the claim that action-only observation matches reward-level observation up to constants is non-obvious. (2) Algorithm-aware inversion of randomized algorithms (TS, EXP3) may be statistically or computationally hard; particle degeneracy could weaken those results, in which case the finding 'randomization is a cheap partial defense' becomes the contribution. (3) The MLE/interval-propagation attack assumes knowledge of the algorithm and its parameters; we will report degradation under algorithm mismatch, but a fully algorithm-agnostic attack may be much weaker. (4) Formal secrecy definitions (mutual information vs. attacker error probability) may not be interchangeable; we will report both and prove relations only where clean. (5) Real-data replay evaluation of bandits is noisy and off-policy; conclusions there are indicative rather than definitive. (6) Non-stationary, contextual, or delayed-feedback settings may substantially change the leakage picture and are left partly to future work.
title: Exploration Is a Broadcast Channel: Property Inference from Bandit Action Logs and the Regret-Secrecy Frontier

evaluation_plan:
1) Predicted-scaling validation (synthetic). K-armed Gaussian and Beta bandits with noise sigma in {0.5, 0.2, 0.05, 0.01} and gaps Delta in {0.3, 0.1, 0.03}, T up to 2e5. Algorithms: (a) full-precision UCB-V/KL-UCB (upper baseline); (b) fixed uniform m-bit quantizer + UCB for m in {1,2,4,8}; (c) 1-bit global dithering (observe 1{X_t > U_t}, U_t ~ Unif[0,1], an unbiased mean oracle) + UCB; (d) proposed AQ-UCB: maintain per-arm mean estimate and confidence width w_a, dither only inside the clipped window [mu_hat_a - c*w_a - c'*sigma_hat_a, mu_hat_a + c*w_a + c'*sigma_hat_a] and de-bias the clipped estimate; (e) shape-aware 1-bit: threshold at the running mean estimate and invert the Gaussian CDF. Metrics: cumulative regret vs t; empirical estimator variance per bit; fitted exponent of regret vs sigma. Prediction to falsify: (b)/(c) plateau at a sigma-independent regret floor while (d)/(e) track (a) within a constant factor.
2) Bit-budget frontier and allocation. Impose a total budget B bits (rather than T rounds) and let each algorithm choose rounds/resolution freely; plot cumulative and simple regret vs B. Include an explicit 'resolution allocator' that solves min_m m*max(sigma_hat_a^2, 4^{-m}) per arm online, testing the rule m* ~ log_4(1/sigma_hat_a^2). Report bits-to-identify-best-arm at 95% confidence and compare to predicted Theta(sigma^2 log(1/sigma)/Delta^2) non-interactive vs Theta(sigma^2/Delta^2) interactive.
3) Interactivity separation, empirically tight. On 2- and 3-armed instances, grid-search over parameterized 1-bit strategies restricted to (i) history-independent quantizers and (ii) history-adaptive quantizers; plot achieved regret against the theoretical lower bound curve to confirm the gap is real and matches constants.
4) Adversarial-to-clipping and heavy-tailed distributions. Bimodal rewards, Bernoulli with rare large payoff, Pareto(alpha=1.5) and lognormal arms. Compare AQ-UCB, 1-bit dithering with a learned dynamic range, truncated-mean UCB and median-of-means UCB. Metric: regret and failure rate; test the claim that coarse feedback matches or beats full precision under heavy tails (quantization as free robustness), and that clipping bias, not variance, is the binding constraint for bimodal rewards.
5) Real-data granularity design. MovieLens-25M and the Open Bandit Dataset via replay. Simulate annotation with L-level scales (L in {2,3,5,10,continuous}), charging log2(L) bits per label under a fixed total bit budget, with annotator noise injected at levels estimated from within-user rating dispersion. Question answered: at a fixed human-annotation bit budget, are many binary judgments better than fewer fine-grained ratings? Check whether the empirically best L matches the theory's noise-matched prediction L* ~ 1/sigma, and whether interactive granularity (coarse early, fine near the top arms) beats any fixed L.
6) Small tie-in: because 1-bit dithered feedback is exactly randomized response, report the locally-private regret obtained 'for free' by AQ-UCB and compare with LDP bandit baselines at matched epsilon.
expected_contribution: (1) Quantization for communication in distributed/federated bandits: 'Solving Multi-Arm Bandit Using a Few Bits of Communication' (Hanna, Yang & Fragouli, AISTATS 2022) and communication-efficient federated bandit papers show that a small fixed number of bits per reward preserves near-optimal *minimax* sqrt(KT) regret. These works fix a quantizer designed by a system engineer to cut network cost; they do not treat resolution as an adaptively controlled decision variable, do not characterize instance-dependent (variance-dependent) bit complexity, and give no lower bounds separating interactive from non-interactive quantization. (2) Variance-adaptive bandits (UCB-V, Bernstein/KL-UCB) and heavy-tailed bandits (Bubeck, Cesa-Bianchi & Lugosi) assume full-precision rewards; we ask what part of their variance adaptivity survives coarse feedback, and show quantization is essentially an implicit robust mean estimator, so coarse feedback can be *better* than fine feedback under heavy tails. (3) One-bit/quantized estimation and interactive vs non-interactive local privacy (Duchi et al.; one-bit compressed sensing; signSGD/QSGD) study estimation or optimization with coarse observations, but never the exploration-measurement coupling: in a bandit, placing a good threshold requires knowing the mean you are trying to estimate, and the arm you must measure precisely changes over time. (4) Dueling/preference bandits and thresholding bandits involve one-bit feedback but with an externally fixed comparison structure; we let the learner *design its own query* (which arm, which threshold, how many bits) under an explicit bit budget. (5) Bandits with censored/binary feedback in operations research assume a fixed censoring level. Our contribution -- a bit-complexity theory with matching upper/lower bounds, an interactivity separation, and an empirical rating-scale design rule for human feedback -- is orthogonal to all of these.
motivation_or_abstract: Bandit theory measures the cost of learning in pulls, implicitly assuming each pull reveals a real number for free. In many deployments the expensive resource is not the pull but the *resolution* of the observation: a human annotator can give a thumbs-up cheaply or a fine-grained score expensively, a sensor can report a coarse bin or a calibrated value, and a client can transmit one bit or a float. We introduce the bit-budgeted bandit, in which the learner selects an arm and a quantizer (a set of at most m bits' worth of measurement questions about the realized reward) each round, and is charged for bits rather than rounds. We develop the resulting bit complexity theory. First, we show that classical variance adaptivity is fragile under blind quantization: with any fixed, history-independent quantizer of m bits, the achievable instance-dependent regret scales with max(sigma^2, 4^{-m}) log T / Delta, so attaining full-precision performance requires Theta(log(1/sigma)) bits per pull -- resolution must be matched to the noise level, not to the gap. Second, we show interactivity removes this cost: an adaptive-window dithering scheme (AQ-UCB) that shrinks its measurement range with its own confidence interval attains sigma^2 log T / Delta regret with a single bit per pull for sub-Gaussian rewards, giving a provable interactive/non-interactive separation. Third, we show quantization is an implicit robust mean estimator, so one-bit feedback matches truncated-mean bandits under heavy tails without moment tuning. Simulations validate the predicted scalings, and replay experiments on recommendation data instantiate the theory as a concrete design rule for how many levels a feedback scale should have.
problem_statement: Sample complexity is the wrong currency when observations are expensive to *measure* rather than to *obtain*: we hypothesize that bandit learning has a distinct bit complexity, that a single adaptively placed bit per pull is enough to match full-precision instance-dependent regret up to constants for sub-Gaussian rewards, and that non-interactive (fixed-resolution) feedback provably needs Theta(log(1/sigma)) bits per pull, yielding a concrete design rule -- feedback resolution should match observation noise, not the reward gap.
proposed_direction: Sample complexity is the wrong currency when observations are expensive to *measure* rather than to *obtain*: we hypothesize that bandit learning has a distinct bit complexity, that a single adaptively placed bit per pull is enough to match full-precision instance-dependent regret up to constants for sub-Gaussian rewards, and that non-interactive (fixed-resolution) feedback provably needs Theta(log(1/sigma)) bits per pull, yielding a concrete design rule -- feedback resolution should match observation noise, not the reward gap.
risks_or_caveats: (1) The unbiased-one-bit trick (dithering) and adaptive one-bit mean estimation are known in estimation and local-privacy literatures; novelty rests on the bandit-specific coupling, the instance-dependent bit-complexity characterization, and the interactivity separation -- if a prior bandit paper already establishes the variance-matched adaptive result, the contribution narrows to lower bounds and the granularity design rule. (2) The non-interactive lower bound must quantify over all m-bit quantizers; a fully general argument may only be provable for restricted classes (e.g., deterministic interval quantizers or location families), in which case we state it for those classes and support the general case empirically. (3) AQ-UCB's clipped-window estimator is biased for non-sub-Gaussian rewards; controlling the bias-variance trade-off inside a confidence-bound analysis may require extra assumptions or a slightly loose log factor. (4) The real-data granularity experiment relies on replayed/off-policy logs and simulated annotator noise, so it is indicative rather than conclusive; multi-annotator noise estimates may be unreliable. (5) The bit-budget model idealizes measurement cost as uniform in bits, whereas human annotation cost may scale non-linearly with scale granularity; we will report sensitivity to alternative cost functions.
title: One Bit Per Pull: The Bit Complexity of Bandit Exploration and the Optimal Granularity of Feedback

evaluation_plan:
1) Scale-fragility audit of real ordinal feedback (no training needed, cheap). Datasets: MovieLens-25M (1-5 stars), Amazon Reviews subsets, Yelp reviews, Open Bandit Dataset (binary, as a control), and public LLM-as-judge score sets (e.g., MT-Bench / AlpacaEval-style 1-10 or Likert judgments). For items/arms with >= n_min observations: (a) fraction of pairs with crossing CDFs (i.e., no first-order dominance) among pairs whose mean gap is 'significant'; (b) reversal rate: fraction of pairs whose mean order flips under some monotone re-encoding of the L levels (an LP feasibility check over the monotone utility polytope) and under a natural family (CRRA/power transforms u(x)=x^gamma, gamma in [0.2,5]); (c) top-arm robustness: is the mean-argmax item FOSD-undominated? how often does the argmax change over gamma? (d) non-transitivity: rate of 3-cycles in the relation P(X_a > X_b) > 1/2 (ties split), and in the mean relation under a common but unknown u. Metric headline: percentage of leaderboard/top-10 rankings that are scale artifacts.
2) Synthetic validation of the theory. K in {3,5,20} arms with L=5 or L=10 level distributions, including a hand-built non-transitive-dice instance and instances sampled to match empirical MovieLens rating shapes; T up to 1e5. Algorithms: (i) UCB on the naive 1..L encoding; (ii) UCB on a mis-specified encoding (power transform); (iii) Copeland/Borda-style dueling-bandit baseline run on simulated pairwise comparisons of sampled rewards; (iv) FOSD screening + uniform play on the undominated set; (v) proposed MR-UCB: per-arm empirical CDFs with simultaneous DKW confidence bands, then solve max_{p in Delta_K} min_{u in U_hat} [ sum_a p_a V_u(a) - max_b V_u(b) ] as an LP (finite L makes U a polytope, V_u linear in u), play p_t, plus optimism by using the most favourable CDF in the band. Metrics: cumulative *robust* regret max_{u in U} regret_u; regret under a hidden ground-truth u; regret under the naive mean (to show what is given up); convergence of the estimated game value to the true value.
3) Randomization gap. On the non-transitive instance and on real-data-fitted triples, compute the exact minimax regret of the best single arm vs. the best mixture; report the gap and verify that MR-UCB's realized robust regret tracks the mixture value while any deterministic rule is linear in T. Grid-search over deterministic policies to confirm tightness.
4) Elicitation complexity. Add a query oracle answering comparisons between two lotteries over levels ('is a sure 3 better than a 50/50 of 1 and 5?'), which is a halfspace cut on the utility polytope. Compare query rules: random cuts, center-of-mass/ellipsoid halving, and our max-regret-reduction rule (query the cut that most reduces current minimax regret, following the current-solution heuristic). Plot achieved max-regret and true-utility regret vs. query budget Q for L in {5,7,10} and K in {5,20,100}; verify the predicted O(L log(1/eps)) scaling and the predicted independence from K and T. Noisy oracle variant: logistic answer noise with repetition; measure robustness and cost inflation.
5) Joint exploration-elicitation trade-off. Fix a combined budget in which one query costs c samples, c in {1,10,100,1000}; compare an interleaved scheduler (query only when the current robust game value exceeds the achievable reduction) against sample-only and query-first baselines. Metric: true-utility cumulative regret at fixed budget.
6) LLM-evaluation case study. Treat K response generators as arms and public judge scores as ordinal rewards; run MR-UCB and mean-UCB in replay. Report how many of the top-5 rankings are FOSD-justified, and how few utility queries (answered by a fixed simulated 'principal' utility, or by a second LLM acting as the principal) are needed to make the ranking scale-robust.
expected_contribution: (1) Preference-based / ordinal bandits: Busa-Fekete et al. (preference-based racing, dueling bandits) and Borda/Copeland dueling-bandit work (Yue & Joachims; Zoghi et al.; Urvoy et al.) study rank-based targets, but they assume the *comparison* relation is given as the feedback channel and adopt a single fixed scale-free target (Borda, Copeland, von Neumann winner) as the definition of optimality. We instead keep standard cardinal bandit feedback, treat the utility as an unknown nuisance object in a monotone class U, define regret as worst-case over U, and show that the choice among Borda/Copeland/mean is itself a modelling assumption that our minimax formulation dispenses with. (2) Risk-aware bandits (CVaR, mean-variance, distributional/quantile bandits) replace the mean with a different fixed functional; they are not scale-free and do not consider sets of utilities. Stochastic-dominance-based selection has appeared in racing algorithms, but only as a partial-order screening rule, with no minimax-regret objective, no randomization result, and no elicitation. (3) Imprecise-reward sequential decision making with active elicitation (Regan & Boutilier, minimax-regret MDPs; Weng & Zanuttini; active preference elicitation for reward learning; RLHF reward modelling) assumes access to the environment model or focuses on offline reward learning; we couple elicitation with *online exploration under bandit feedback* and give a sample/query complexity split. (4) Reward-scale sensitivity of LLM-as-judge leaderboards has been noted empirically but never framed as an identifiability problem in sequential decision making with matching upper and lower bounds. Our contributions -- an unavoidability result driven by non-transitive-dice constructions, a game-theoretic randomized minimax-regret algorithm operating on CDF confidence bands, an elicitation-complexity theorem, and a large empirical audit of real ordinal feedback -- are new.
motivation_or_abstract: Bandit algorithms maximize the mean of a number, but in most applications that number is an arbitrary encoding of an ordinal signal: a five-star rating, a 1-10 LLM-judge score, a clinical severity grade. Mapping stars to utilities as 1,2,3,4,5 rather than 1,2,3,4,10 is a modelling choice that no one validates, and it can flip which arm is best. We formalize the monotone-robust bandit: rewards take values in an ordered set of L levels, the true utility u is an unknown increasing function, and the learner is judged by regret maximized over all utilities consistent with what it knows. First, we characterize identifiability: an arm is optimal for every utility exactly when it first-order stochastically dominates the others, and we show, via non-transitive-dice constructions, that the pairwise majority relation among arm distributions can cycle. Consequently any algorithm that only samples rewards -- however many -- must incur linear worst-case regret if it commits to a single arm, whereas a randomized mixture provably attains a strictly smaller minimax regret given by the value of a zero-sum game between the learner and the utility. We give MR-UCB, which maintains DKW-style CDF confidence bands, solves the induced robust game by a linear program, and plays the maximin mixture; it attains sublinear regret with respect to the game value, with rates governed by a dominance gap rather than a mean gap. Second, we add a second feedback channel: standard-gamble queries about the utility scale. We prove O(L log(1/eps)) queries -- independent of the number of arms and horizon -- suffice for eps-max-regret, give a query lower bound, and a max-regret-reduction query rule. Finally, we audit MovieLens, Amazon reviews, Yelp and public LLM-judge scores, quantifying how often mean-based rankings and leaderboards are scale artifacts.
problem_statement: Almost every deployed bandit optimizes the mean of an arbitrarily chosen numerical encoding of an ordinal signal (1-5 stars, 1-10 judge scores, clinical grades), yet the identity of the best arm is *not* invariant to monotone re-encodings of that signal; we hypothesize (i) such rank reversals and even non-transitive dominance cycles are common in real logged feedback, (ii) no algorithm that only samples rewards can resolve them, so a scale-free learner must play a randomized minimax-regret mixture over arms, and (iii) a handful of cheap utility-elicitation queries (O(L log 1/eps) standard-gamble comparisons over the L observation levels, independent of the number of arms and the horizon) suffices to recover near-optimal single-arm performance.
proposed_direction: Almost every deployed bandit optimizes the mean of an arbitrarily chosen numerical encoding of an ordinal signal (1-5 stars, 1-10 judge scores, clinical grades), yet the identity of the best arm is *not* invariant to monotone re-encodings of that signal; we hypothesize (i) such rank reversals and even non-transitive dominance cycles are common in real logged feedback, (ii) no algorithm that only samples rewards can resolve them, so a scale-free learner must play a randomized minimax-regret mixture over arms, and (iii) a handful of cheap utility-elicitation queries (O(L log 1/eps) standard-gamble comparisons over the L observation levels, independent of the number of arms and the horizon) suffices to recover near-optimal single-arm performance.
risks_or_caveats: (1) First-order stochastic dominance and Borda/Copeland targets already exist in the bandit literature; the novelty rests on the minimax-regret-over-utilities objective, the randomization result, and elicitation complexity. If a prior work already couples elicitation with bandit exploration, the contribution narrows to the empirical audit and the game-theoretic algorithm. (2) The audit's conclusions depend on the monotone class U: with fully unconstrained monotone utilities, non-comparability may be so pervasive that results look vacuous; we will therefore report a graded family of constraint sets (unconstrained monotone, bounded-curvature, CRRA) and treat the amount of structure needed for identifiability as a finding rather than an assumption. (3) DKW-band-based confidence sets give conservative constants; instance-dependent optimality may require more delicate analysis, and our regret bound may be off by log factors from a matching lower bound. (4) Real logged ratings are heavily confounded (self-selection, popularity bias), so reversal rates measure the fragility of the observed distributions rather than causal effects; we will note this and include a bias-robustness check on subsets with dense observations. (5) The elicitation oracle assumes a coherent expected-utility principal; violations (framing effects, non-EU preferences) would invalidate the standard-gamble cuts, though the sampling-only minimax results remain valid. (6) Extending to continuous rewards or contextual/linear settings requires discretization and is only partially addressed.
title: Whose Scale Is It Anyway? Monotone-Robust Bandits with Utility Elicitation

evaluation_plan:
1) Benchmark construction. Six drift families: (a) label remapping (SST-2/AGNews/TREC with verbalizer set A then B, including full flips and permutations); (b) in-context linear regression (y=w_A^T x then y=w_B^T x, controllable angle between w_A,w_B) evaluated on numeric-token LLMs and small trained transformers; (c) boolean/rule induction (e.g., parity over different index subsets); (d) output-format switch (JSON -> XML, uppercase -> lowercase); (e) input-language or translation-target switch; (f) preference reversal (prefer concise -> prefer verbose). Grid over n_pre in {0,2,4,8,16,32,64} x n_post in {1,2,4,8,16,32} with 200+ prompts per cell. Models: Llama-3.1-8B/70B-Instruct (and base), Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B/14B, Mistral-7B, Gemma-2-9B, OLMo-2 (for pretraining-data transparency), plus GPT-4o-mini via API for a closed-model check.
2) Reference-learner comparison. Fit (i) an exchangeable Bayesian posterior over the finite rule set given all demos, (ii) a geometrically discounted likelihood learner with discount gamma, (iii) a last-k-only learner. Metric: which predicts model accuracy/logit ratios best (log-likelihood, R^2) and the implied gamma per model/scale. Primary quantitative test of the switch-cost law: regress post-switch accuracy on n_post/(n_pre+n_post) vs. on n_post alone; report 'adaptation half-life' h(n_pre) = number of post-switch demos to reach 50% of oracle (n_pre=0) accuracy, and test h ~ c * n_pre (linear) vs. constant.
3) Mechanistic analysis. Extract task vectors for rule A and rule B from clean stationary prompts (mean residual-stream activation at the final delimiter, per layer). For drifted prompts, regress the observed activation onto span{v_A, v_B} and test whether the fitted weight on v_B matches n_post/(n_pre+n_post). Identify task-encoding heads by (i) attention mass on demonstration label tokens, (ii) causal patching: replace head outputs with clean rule-B-prompt outputs and measure recovered post-switch accuracy. Also train a per-layer linear probe on the residual stream to classify 'a rule change has occurred in this context' and measure detection latency vs. behavioral adaptation latency (does the model 'know' before it acts?).
4) Interventions (all training-free, evaluated on held-out drift families). (a) Prompt-level: explicit instruction 'the rule changed; use only the most recent examples'; also re-stating recent demos. (b) Attention discounting: add log(gamma) * (number of demonstration blocks between query and key) to attention logits, applied only in the identified task-encoding heads; sweep gamma in [0.5,1.0]; ablate 'all heads' vs 'task heads' vs 'random heads'. (c) Probe-gated discounting: apply (b) only when the drift probe fires, so stationary prompts are unaffected. (d) KV-block eviction: drop pre-switch demonstration KV entries as an upper-bound oracle. Metrics: post-switch accuracy vs. oracle rule-B-only prompt, stationary-ICL regression (accuracy on 20 standard ICL tasks with no drift), false-positive rate of the probe, and compute overhead.
5) Small-model pretraining study (stability-plasticity). Train ~10M-parameter GPT-2-style transformers from scratch on synthetic ICL tasks (linear regression, sparse parity) with meta-training mixtures containing p in {0, 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 1.0} fraction of drifting sequences (one or more mid-sequence task switches). Measure (i) post-switch adaptation half-life, (ii) stationary in-context sample efficiency, (iii) implied discount gamma, and (iv) whether induction-head-like circuits become recency-gated. This tests whether stale-evidence anchoring is a consequence of stationary pretraining data rather than an architectural limit.
6) Optional realism check: multi-turn instruction-revision dialogues (revised constraints after several compliant turns) scored with an LLM judge and rule-based checkers, testing whether the same switch-cost law appears in naturalistic settings.
expected_contribution: Almost all ICL analysis assumes a *single stationary* latent task per prompt: Bayesian views and Bayesian scaling laws (Xie et al. 2022; Arora et al. 2024), task recognition vs. task learning (Pan et al. 2023; Lin & Lee 2024), context-scaling analyses (2025), concept encoding-decoding and task/function vectors (Todd et al. 2024; Hendel et al. 2023; From Context to Concept, 2025), and order/permutation sensitivity work (Lu et al. 2022; Rethinking Invariance in ICL, 2025) which explicitly treats demonstrations as exchangeable and even engineers permutation invariance. Robustness work studies *noisy or shifted candidate pools* (ConDS, 2025) and spurious features in ICL, but the noise is i.i.d. across the context, not a structured mid-context change of the ground-truth rule. Flipped-label studies (Wei et al. 2023) flip labels for the *whole* prompt. In-context RL (Algorithm Distillation, DPT, in-context model-based planning) handles non-stationary environments but measures return, not the evidence-integration rule, and offers no mechanistic account for pretrained LLMs. Our contribution is distinct on three axes: (i) we introduce mid-context task drift as a diagnostic regime that directly separates exchangeable-Bayes from recency-weighted accounts of ICL — a distinction invisible in stationary prompts; (ii) we predict and test a quantitative 'switch-cost law' relating adaptation to pre-switch example count; (iii) we derive a training-free intervention (head-selective attention discounting triggered by a drift probe) from the diagnosis, turning permutation invariance from a desideratum into an identified failure mode.
motivation_or_abstract: In-context learning is almost universally studied with prompts drawn from a single stationary task, and the field has even sought permutation-invariant ICL algorithms. Yet real contexts drift: instructions get revised mid-conversation, user preferences change, tool APIs update, and streaming data shifts. We ask a simple question: what does an LLM do when the labeling rule changes in the middle of its context? We construct a controlled benchmark of drifting prompts (label remappings, in-context linear regression with a changing weight vector, boolean-function switches, output-format and language switches, and preference reversals) in which the first n_pre demonstrations follow rule A and the next n_post follow rule B, and we compare model predictions against two reference learners: an exchangeable Bayesian posterior over rules (which cannot discount stale evidence) and a recency-discounted learner. We find and characterize 'stale-evidence anchoring': post-switch accuracy is governed by the *ratio* n_post/(n_pre+n_post) rather than by absolute recency, so more pre-switch evidence makes adaptation proportionally slower — a distinct scaling law from stationary ICL curves. Mechanistically, we show via task-vector probes and logit lens that the model's internal task representation after a switch is a count-weighted convex blend of the two task encodings, and that a small set of task-encoding heads carries this blend. Finally, we show that a training-free intervention — exponential attention-logit discounting over demonstration blocks in those heads, gated by a linear 'drift detector' probe read off the residual stream — recovers most of the oracle post-switch accuracy while leaving stationary ICL intact. Small-transformer pretraining experiments reveal a stability-plasticity tradeoff: meta-training with drifting contexts yields recency-adaptive ICL at a measurable cost in stationary sample efficiency.
problem_statement: Because ICL behaves like an (approximately) exchangeable Bayesian learner over latent tasks, LLMs cannot discount obsolete demonstrations: when the labeling rule changes in the middle of a context, the cost of adapting scales with the *number* of pre-switch examples rather than their recency, and the model's internal task representation becomes a count-weighted blend of old and new tasks. If this diagnosis is right, then injecting a purely inference-time recency prior into a small set of task-encoding attention heads should restore adaptivity without harming stationary ICL.
proposed_direction: Because ICL behaves like an (approximately) exchangeable Bayesian learner over latent tasks, LLMs cannot discount obsolete demonstrations: when the labeling rule changes in the middle of a context, the cost of adapting scales with the *number* of pre-switch examples rather than their recency, and the model's internal task representation becomes a count-weighted blend of old and new tasks. If this diagnosis is right, then injecting a purely inference-time recency prior into a small set of task-encoding attention heads should restore adaptivity without harming stationary ICL.
risks_or_caveats: (1) Models may already be strongly recency-biased, so no anchoring appears; this is still a publishable negative result that overturns the exchangeable-Bayes picture, and the reference-learner fits quantify gamma either way. (2) Instruction-tuned models may over-rely on the most recent example, confounding drift adaptation with generic recency bias — controlled by including within-rule order permutations and matched no-drift controls. (3) Task vectors may not be linearly decomposable into span{v_A,v_B}; we report subspace-fit quality and fall back to logit-difference-based mixture estimates. (4) Attention discounting may hurt long-range copying and instruction following; mitigated by head selectivity, probe gating, and explicit stationary-regression evaluation. (5) Some drift families are semantically confusable with noisy labels; we include a noisy-label control (same number of 'wrong' labels but interleaved rather than blocked) to show blocked drift is qualitatively different. (6) Compute limits us to <=14B open models locally plus small API checks; scale trends may be incomplete.
title: When the Rule Changes Mid-Prompt: Stale-Evidence Anchoring in In-Context Learning and a Cheap Cure

evaluation_plan:
1) Information-matched benchmark. Tasks: (a) binary classification (SST-2, AGNews restricted to 2 classes, RTE, BoolQ) where each demo is rendered either positively ('Input: x / Label: positive') or negatively ('Input: x / Label: NOT negative'), with the label set stated in the instruction so the two are logically equivalent; (b) k-way classification (TREC k=6, Banking77 subsets k=4/8/16, synthetic color/shape categories) with negative demos excluding one wrong label; (c) synthetic rule induction with an explicit finite hypothesis space (boolean concepts over 5 features, ~100 candidate rules) where positive and negative examples can be exactly information-matched by Bayesian bit count; (d) constraint tasks (generate a word satisfying constraints, with negative demos = rejected candidates). Grid over n_demos in {0,2,4,8,16,32}, 300 prompts per cell, 5 prompt formats and 3 negation phrasings ('NOT', 'is wrong', 'incorrect answer:') to separate wording from mechanism. Models: Qwen2.5-0.5/1.5/7/14B, Llama-3.1-8B & 70B (base and instruct), Gemma-2-9B, OLMo-2-7B, plus GPT-4o-mini/Claude-Haiku API checks.
2) Primary metrics. Negative-Evidence Efficiency NEE = (acc_neg - acc_0)/(acc_pos - acc_0) at matched information. Bits-extracted: fit accuracy as a function of Bayesian-oracle posterior entropy reduction for positive and negative streams; report the ratio of effective bits. Negation-as-association test: sign and magnitude of Δlogit for the *excluded* label relative to the no-demo baseline (per-model, bootstrap CIs). Also report mixed prompts (m positive + n negative) to test additivity.
3) Bayesian-oracle comparison. Exact posterior over the finite hypothesis space for tasks (a) and (c); plot model accuracy vs oracle accuracy as a function of demo count, separately for positive-only, negative-only, and mixed streams. This yields the headline figure: positive ICL tracks the oracle; negative ICL saturates far below it.
4) Mechanistic analysis (on 7-9B models with hooks). (i) Per-head direct logit attribution to the excluded label token; identify heads whose output writes *toward* the negated label. (ii) Attention pattern analysis: does head attention to the demo answer token change when the polarity marker flips? Quantify a polarity-sensitivity score per head. (iii) Linear probes at each layer on the residual stream at the delimiter for 'the last demo was negative' — measure whether polarity is linearly decodable (information present) despite behavioral insensitivity (routing failure). (iv) Causal patching: patch polarity-probe direction or specific head outputs from a matched positive prompt and measure behavioral change; also ablate copy-suppression heads (McDougall-style) to test whether they are the missing machinery.
5) Training-free interventions, evaluated on held-out tasks. (a) Verbalized elimination: an instruction plus one worked example telling the model to first rewrite each negative demo as the implied positive statement (and a CoT variant). (b) Hypothesis-space masking: constrained decoding that zeroes labels explicitly excluded by negative demos (upper bound / sanity oracle). (c) Polarity-gated copy inversion: for tokens inside negative demos, negate the contribution of the top-K identified copy heads to the label logits (implemented as a hook that subtracts the head's OV write on demo answer tokens), gated by the polarity probe; sweep K and gate threshold. Metrics: recovered fraction of oracle gap, degradation on 20 standard positive-only ICL tasks (must be ~0), and compute overhead.
6) Small-model meta-training study. Train ~10-20M parameter transformers from scratch on synthetic ICL rule-induction sequences with fraction p in {0, 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 1.0} of negative-labeled examples. Measure (i) whether eliminative ICL emerges and at what p, (ii) sample efficiency of positive vs negative evidence, (iii) whether anti-induction / suppression heads appear (head-level copying score over training), (iv) transfer: does training with negative evidence on one rule family generalize to unseen families? This tests data-distribution vs architecture explanations.
7) Agentic application. Multi-turn setting on GSM8K, ARC-Challenge, and a simple tool-calling environment where the context contains the model's k previous *wrong* answers labeled as wrong. Metric: exact-repetition rate of a previously-listed wrong answer vs. a no-history control matched for token count (filled with irrelevant text), and accuracy. Then apply intervention (5a/5c) and re-measure. This links the mechanistic deficit to the widely reported failure of self-correction loops.
expected_contribution: Four literatures touch this but none isolate it. (1) Negation in LMs: Kassner & Schütze (2020), Ettinger (2020), Hosseini et al. (2021), and inverse-scaling on negated prompts (Jang et al. 2023) show LMs mishandle negation in *task instructions or single sentences*; we instead ask whether negation can serve as *learning signal inside demonstrations*, an evidence-integration question rather than a semantic-comprehension one. (2) Label-corruption ICL: Min et al. (2022) show random labels barely hurt; Wei et al. (2023) study flipped labels; Yoo et al. (2022) revisit ground-truth sensitivity. Crucially, in all of these the wrong labels are *unmarked* — the model is never told an example is a counterexample, so nothing tests eliminative inference. Our negative demos are explicitly marked and are information-equivalent to positive ones by construction. (3) Contrastive/negative-example prompting methods (c-ICL, contrastive CoT, 'learning from mistakes' prompts) *engineer* gains from positive+negative pairs but report only end-task accuracy; they never ask how many bits of the available eliminative information the model actually uses, nor why it fails, and they confound the negative signal with extra tokens/content. (4) Bayesian accounts of ICL (Xie et al. 2022; Bayesian scaling laws, Arora et al. 2024) and concept/task-vector mechanisms assume positive i.i.d. (x,y) evidence; a Bayesian learner handles negative evidence for free, so our design is a sharp falsification test of the Bayesian story that stationary positive-only prompts cannot provide. We additionally connect the deficit to a concrete circuit story (induction/copy heads and copy-suppression heads, Olsson et al. 2022; McDougall et al. 2023) and to a practical failure: agents that keep past wrong answers in context repeat them.
motivation_or_abstract: Every study of in-context learning feeds the model positive evidence: examples of what the answer *is*. Human and Bayesian learners also learn from what the answer is *not*. We ask a simple question with a clean experimental handle: can LLMs learn in-context from explicitly negative demonstrations, and if not, why? Our key design is information matching. In a binary task, 'x is NOT negative' is logically identical to 'x is positive', so a negative demonstration carries exactly the same bits as a positive one; in a k-way task, a negative demonstration carries a precisely computable log(k/(k-1)) bits. This lets us define negative-evidence efficiency, the fraction of available eliminative information an LLM converts into accuracy, and to compare directly against a Bayesian oracle. Across open models (Qwen2.5, Llama-3.1, Gemma-2, OLMo-2, 0.5B-70B) and synthetic rule-induction, classification, and constraint-satisfaction tasks, we predict and test a strong asymmetry: negative demonstrations yield a small fraction of the gain of information-equivalent positive ones, and often *raise* the probability of the very label they exclude — negation-as-association. Mechanistically, we attribute this to label-copying induction heads that attend to the demonstration answer token while remaining largely insensitive to the polarity marker, showing via per-head logit attribution, polarity probes, and causal patching where polarity information exists but fails to be routed into suppression. We then repair the deficit training-free: (i) verbalized elimination that rewrites negative demos into positive ones, and (ii) polarity-gated inversion of copy-head contributions, recovering most of the oracle gap. Finally, small-transformer meta-training shows eliminative ICL emerges only when pretraining data contains negative evidence, and coincides with the birth of anti-induction heads. As an application, we show that keeping past wrong answers in an agent's context increases repetition of those exact errors, and that our fix reduces it.
problem_statement: In-context learning is driven by positive label copying (induction/copy heads), so LLMs extract far less information from *negative* (eliminative) demonstrations than from information-equivalent positive ones — and in the limit they treat 'x is NOT y' as evidence *for* y. We test this with an exactly information-matched positive-vs-negative demonstration design (in binary tasks a negative demo is logically identical to a positive one), quantify the shortfall in bits relative to a Bayesian oracle, localize it to copy-suppression-deficient heads, and repair it training-free.
proposed_direction: In-context learning is driven by positive label copying (induction/copy heads), so LLMs extract far less information from *negative* (eliminative) demonstrations than from information-equivalent positive ones — and in the limit they treat 'x is NOT y' as evidence *for* y. We test this with an exactly information-matched positive-vs-negative demonstration design (in binary tasks a negative demo is logically identical to a positive one), quantify the shortfall in bits relative to a Bayesian oracle, localize it to copy-suppression-deficient heads, and repair it training-free.
risks_or_caveats: (1) Strong instruction-tuned models may already handle explicit negation well on easy binary tasks, compressing NEE toward 1; we mitigate by including k-way and multi-negative-demo regimes where eliminative inference must be composed, and by reporting scale trends (the interesting result may be that NEE grows with scale but stays sub-Bayesian). (2) Negation phrasing is a confound; addressed with three phrasings, a symbol-only marker (e.g., 'x → y [✗]'), and format randomization. (3) Information matching is exact only when the label set is closed and stated; for open-ended constraint tasks we report qualitative rather than bit-level comparisons. (4) Copy-head attribution may be diffuse in larger models, weakening the mechanistic claim; we pre-register the probe/patching analysis as the primary mechanistic evidence with head attribution as support, and run mechanistic work on ≤9B models. (5) Interventions on attention writes may destabilize generation; we restrict them to demo answer-token positions and verify perplexity on held-out text. (6) Compute limits local hook-based work to ≤14B models; 70B and API models are behavioral-only.
title: What LLMs Fail to Learn From What Isn't So: Eliminative In-Context Learning and the Copy-Head Bottleneck

evaluation_plan:
1) Benchmark of nested-hypothesis concept learning (4 domains, all with explicitly enumerable hypothesis spaces so exact Bayesian references can be computed). (a) Number game: domain 1-100, hypothesis space of ~60 mathematical (multiples, powers, primes, ranges) and interval hypotheses, matching Tenenbaum's setup so published human generalization data can be used as a baseline. (b) Taxonomic categories: examples like {dalmatian} vs {dalmatian, poodle, beagle, corgi}; probes at subordinate/basic/superordinate levels (WordNet-derived, with hypothesis sizes estimated from WordNet extension counts). (c) String/regex induction: strings consistent with both a narrow pattern (e.g., 'a^n b^n') and a broad one ('contains a and b'); hypothesis sizes computed exactly over bounded-length strings. (d) Label-scope classification: an ICL prompt gives k positive examples of a category label (all drawn from a narrow subcategory) and we measure whether the model applies the label to superordinate items - the practical face of overgeneralization.
2) Core manipulation and metric. For each item, vary n in {1,2,3,4,6,8} where all examples are consistent with both narrow and broad hypotheses and (critically) are *maximally uninformative individually* (no example excludes the broad hypothesis). Elicit generalization probabilities for held-out probe items via next-token yes/no logits (and a verbalized-probability variant). Primary quantity: narrowing slope = d/dn of P(probe in concept) for broad-only probes. Fit the one-parameter Bayesian family with likelihood proportional to 1/|h|^alpha and prior fixed from the enumerated hypothesis space; report maximum-likelihood alpha_hat with bootstrap CIs per model, per domain. Secondary: KL divergence of model generalization gradients from alpha=0 and alpha=1 Bayes; correlation with human data for the number game. Also run a 'redundancy control': repeating the *same* example n times (which should not narrow under any account) to verify the measured narrowing is not a token-frequency artifact.
3) Sampling-frame causal test. Hold examples fixed and vary a one-sentence frame: (i) 'A teacher chose these examples to help you identify the rule as precisely as possible' (strong/pedagogical), (ii) 'These examples were encountered at random while browsing' (weak), (iii) 'A teacher chose these examples but is only allowed to show positive examples' (strong), (iv) no frame. A normative learner shifts alpha between 0 and 1; measure delta alpha_hat per frame. Also test a 'teacher stopped here' cue ('the teacher showed only these') vs 'more examples exist'.
4) Scale and model family sweep. Qwen2.5 0.5/1.5/7/14B, Llama-3.1-8B/70B (base and instruct), Gemma-2-2B/9B, OLMo-2-7B, plus GPT-4o-mini and Claude-Haiku via API. Questions: does alpha_hat grow with scale? Does instruction tuning or RLHF change it? Does reasoning-style prompting (CoT) or a reasoning model (e.g., a distilled R1) change it? Base-vs-instruct comparison separates pretraining statistics from alignment.
5) Small-transformer meta-training study (origin of alpha). Train ~10-20M parameter decoder-only transformers on synthetic in-context concept learning over a known hypothesis space (nested intervals / divisibility rules over a discrete domain) under three data-generating processes: (i) strong sampling (examples drawn i.i.d. uniformly from the true concept's extension), (ii) weak sampling (x drawn uniformly from the domain, then labeled +/-, with only positives shown), (iii) mixtures with fraction p strong. Estimate alpha_hat of the trained model on held-out concepts. Prediction: (i) yields alpha near 1, (ii) yields alpha near 0, and alpha_hat increases monotonically with p. Additional condition: append an explicit sampling-frame token to sequences to test whether a model can learn to *condition* alpha on metadata - the trainable analogue of Experiment 3, telling us whether the LLM failure is 'cannot represent' or 'never had to'.
6) Training-free repairs, evaluated on held-out domains. (a) Hypothesis-enumeration CoT: instruct the model to list candidate rules, estimate each rule's extension size, and prefer smaller extensions when all rules fit; (b) size-scored reranking: sample candidate rules from the model, compute/ask for extension sizes, score by n*log(1/|h|) + log prior, and answer with the argmax (a scaffolded Bayesian learner); (c) self-generated probes: model proposes discriminating test items and answers as if it observed the teacher's silence. Metrics: recovered alpha_hat, human-correlation on number game, false-positive rate on superordinate probes in the label-scope task, and cost in tokens. Control that repairs do not hurt standard ICL classification accuracy on 15 conventional tasks.
7) Practical consequence for demonstration selection. Using standard similarity retrievers (SBERT/BM25) on classification datasets, measure how often the retrieved k-shot set is consistent with a narrow-but-wrong hypothesis (e.g., all retrieved positives share a spurious surface feature), and show that LLMs fail to narrow when narrowing is correct and fail to broaden when the retrieved set is unrepresentative. Compare 'diversity-sampled' vs 'similarity-retrieved' demonstrations under our alpha framework to give a principled reinterpretation of known selection heuristics.
expected_contribution: (1) Bayesian views of ICL: Xie et al. (2022) implicit Bayesian inference; Bayesian scaling laws for ICL (Arora et al., 2024); Bayes' Power for Explaining ICL Generalizations (2025); task recognition vs. task learning (Pan et al., 2023; Lin & Lee, 2024). All of these assume a likelihood form and fit accuracy/posterior-concentration curves; none identifies *which sampling assumption* the model's implicit likelihood encodes, even though this is the single degree of freedom that determines whether more consistent examples sharpen a hypothesis at all. (2) Cognitive science: Tenenbaum & Griffiths' number game and the size principle, Xu & Tenenbaum's word learning, and pedagogical/teaching-by-example models (Shafto, Goodman & Griffiths). Recent cognitive-science probes have run GPT-style models on number-game-like items, but they report accuracy or qualitative similarity to humans on fixed example sets; they do not (a) estimate the sampling exponent, (b) causally manipulate the sampling frame while holding the examples fixed, or (c) connect the result to pretraining data statistics or to practical ICL. (3) ICL demonstration selection (similarity retrieval, ambiguity-aware selection, ConDS) implicitly *is* pedagogical sampling: a retriever hand-picks examples. Our results imply a mismatch between how demonstrations are produced (curated) and how models interpret them (as random observations), which no prior work articulates or tests. (4) Mechanistic ICL work (concept encoding-decoding, contextualize-then-aggregate, task vectors) explains how task information is aggregated but not what statistical assumption governs aggregation. Our contribution is a falsifiable, one-parameter characterization of ICL's implicit likelihood, a within-item causal test using sampling-frame metadata, a data-distributional explanation via small-transformer meta-training, and a training-free repair.
motivation_or_abstract: Given the examples {16, 8, 2, 64}, humans confidently infer 'powers of two' rather than 'even numbers', because a random sample of even numbers would be a suspicious coincidence. This inference requires a specific likelihood - the size principle, p(x|h) proportional to 1/|h| - which follows from assuming examples were drawn from *within* the concept (strong or pedagogical sampling). Every Bayesian account of in-context learning posits a posterior over latent tasks, yet none has asked which sampling assumption LLMs encode. We answer this with a simple, quantitative probe: we present LLMs with nested-hypothesis concept-learning prompts (numbers, taxonomic categories, regexes/string patterns, and label-scope classification) in which the examples are consistent with both a narrow and a broad hypothesis, vary the number of consistent examples n from 1 to 8, and measure the generalization gradient over probe items that discriminate the hypotheses. Fitting a one-parameter Bayesian family with likelihood 1/|h|^alpha to model behavior yields an interpretable 'sampling exponent'. Our central prediction is that LLMs sit near alpha = 0 (weak sampling): breadth is driven by surface similarity to the examples, not by the improbability of the coincidence, so redundant consistent examples buy almost no narrowing - unlike humans, who track alpha near 1. We further test whether alpha is a controllable knob by stating the sampling frame explicitly ('a teacher chose these to be maximally informative' vs 'these were randomly encountered'), which changes the normative answer while holding examples fixed. We then explain the deficit: small transformers meta-trained on positive-only strongly-sampled concepts do acquire alpha near 1, whereas incidental/weakly-sampled meta-training yields alpha near 0, indicating a data-distributional rather than architectural origin. Finally, we show a cheap repair (hypothesis-enumeration-with-size CoT) that recovers most human-like narrowing and reduces overgeneralization in a practical rule-induction task, and we show that similarity-based demonstration retrieval systematically produces prompts whose pedagogical information LLMs cannot exploit.
problem_statement: Bayesian accounts of ICL specify a posterior over latent tasks but never test the *likelihood* that generates demonstrations. We hypothesize that LLMs implicitly assume demonstrations are weakly sampled (randomly observed) rather than strongly/pedagogically sampled (deliberately chosen from within the target concept), so they do not obey the size principle: their generalization breadth barely narrows as more mutually-consistent examples arrive, whereas humans and strong-sampling Bayes narrow exponentially. We can measure this as a single interpretable exponent alpha in p(x|h) ~ 1/|h|^alpha estimated from model behavior, show alpha ~ 0 for LLMs, show alpha is largely insensitive to explicit statements about how examples were chosen, and show alpha ~ 1 emerges in small transformers only when meta-training data are actually strongly sampled.
proposed_direction: Bayesian accounts of ICL specify a posterior over latent tasks but never test the *likelihood* that generates demonstrations. We hypothesize that LLMs implicitly assume demonstrations are weakly sampled (randomly observed) rather than strongly/pedagogically sampled (deliberately chosen from within the target concept), so they do not obey the size principle: their generalization breadth barely narrows as more mutually-consistent examples arrive, whereas humans and strong-sampling Bayes narrow exponentially. We can measure this as a single interpretable exponent alpha in p(x|h) ~ 1/|h|^alpha estimated from model behavior, show alpha ~ 0 for LLMs, show alpha is largely insensitive to explicit statements about how examples were chosen, and show alpha ~ 1 emerges in small transformers only when meta-training data are actually strongly sampled.
risks_or_caveats: (1) Strong models may already display size-principle-like narrowing on the number game because that dataset and Tenenbaum's analysis are in pretraining data; mitigated by the novel regex/string, taxonomic, and label-scope domains with randomized surface forms, and by a contamination check (asking models to recall the paradigm). (2) alpha_hat is only identifiable given a hypothesis space and prior; we fix these to the standard enumerations, report sensitivity to prior choice, and additionally report model-free narrowing slopes that require no fitted prior. (3) Eliciting calibrated generalization probabilities from LLMs is noisy; addressed via logit-based yes/no with format randomization, order-balanced probes, verbalized-probability and forced-choice replications, and multiple paraphrases. (4) A null result on the sampling-frame manipulation is possible but informative (it shows the sampling assumption is not a controllable knob, motivating training-side fixes and connecting to Experiment 5). (5) Small-transformer results may not transfer to LLM scale; we present them as a mechanistic existence proof about data distributions, not a claim about LLM training. (6) Extension sizes for natural-language categories are only approximate; we use WordNet counts plus human-annotated size rankings and report rank-based analyses robust to size mis-estimation.
title: Suspicious Coincidences Are Not Suspicious to LLMs: Testing the Sampling Assumption Behind In-Context Learning

evaluation_plan:
1) Stochastic ICL benchmark (exact ground truth). Families: (a) Bernoulli label noise on classification: a real task (SST-2, AG News, RTE, TREC) whose demonstration labels are resampled so that the true rule holds with probability p in {0.5,0.6,0.7,0.8,0.9,1.0}; (b) pure abstract rules with no semantic prior (tokens 'foo'/'bar' assigned to symbolic inputs with rate p), which removes the model's pretraining prior as a confound; (c) coin/urn tasks (context lists outcomes of a biased process; query asks for the next outcome); (d) in-context regression with known observation noise (y = w x + noise, sigma varied), scored by whether sampled/verbalized predictions match the correct predictive spread; (e) heteroscedastic variant, where p depends on an observable feature of x (e.g., p=0.9 for inputs of type 1 and p=0.6 for type 2, or p varying with a stated attribute). Grid: n_demos in {2,4,8,16,32,64,128}, 300 prompts per cell, 4 prompt formats, label-word and order randomization. Models: Qwen2.5 0.5/1.5/7/14B, Llama-3.1-8B and 70B (base and instruct), Gemma-2-2B/9B, OLMo-2-7B, plus GPT-4o-mini / Claude-Haiku behavioral checks (logprobs where available, else repeated sampling to estimate the distribution).
2) Primary metrics. (i) Aleatoric transmission coefficient beta: regress model log-odds of the majority label on the exact posterior-predictive log-odds (Beta-Bernoulli with uniform prior over the empirical context) across all (p, n) cells; report beta with bootstrap CIs, plus intercept (bias) and R^2. Predict beta << 1. (ii) Epistemic sensitivity epsilon: for p=1.0, slope of model log-odds vs. log n, compared with the Bayesian slope. (iii) Distributional error: KL(oracle || model) and ECE-against-oracle. (iv) Sampling test: does temperature-1 sampling recover the frequency p (probability matching) or collapse (maximizing)? (v) Marginal-vs-conditional control: prompts where the label marginal is 0.5 but conditional rates differ by input type, to verify the model is not merely copying the global base rate. (vi) Heteroscedastic score: per-group beta in family (e).
3) Behavioral controls and simple prompting baselines. Does an explicit statement of the noise ('labels are noisy about 30% of the time') fix it? Does an instruction to output a probability, or a verbalized-counting CoT ('count how many demonstrations of each label, then give the fraction'), fix it? Does many-shot (128 demos) help or hurt? Does instruction tuning change beta (base vs. instruct)? These separate 'cannot represent' from 'does not by default'.
4) Mechanistic analysis (7-9B models with hooks). Train ridge/logistic probes at every layer on the residual stream at the final delimiter to predict the in-context noise rate p (and, in the heteroscedastic case, the group-specific rate), using held-out p values and held-out tasks; report R^2 by layer as evidence for encoded-but-unused noise information. Causal tests: (i) patch the probe direction from a high-noise prompt into a low-noise prompt and measure the change in output entropy; (ii) per-head direct logit attribution to the minority label to find whether copy/induction heads dominate and drive collapse; (iii) ablate top copy heads and re-measure beta.
5) Training-free repairs, evaluated on held-out task families. (a) Activation steering: add alpha * (decoded noise direction) to the residual stream, with alpha calibrated once on a synthetic development set; (b) probe-conditioned affine logit recalibration: rescale label logits by a temperature that is an affine function of the probe's decoded noise rate; (c) scaffolded counting oracle (upper bound). Metrics: recovered beta and KL to oracle, plus a strict no-regression check on 15 standard clean ICL tasks (accuracy must be unchanged) and negligible latency overhead.
6) Small-transformer meta-training control. Train ~10-20M-parameter decoder-only transformers on synthetic ICL sequences whose tasks are (i) deterministic only, (ii) stochastic with p sampled per sequence, (iii) mixtures with fraction q stochastic. Measure beta, epsilon, and heteroscedastic learning as a function of q. Prediction: beta near 1 emerges only with stochastic meta-training, establishing a data-distributional origin, and providing a reference for what a well-calibrated in-context learner looks like at small scale.
7) Real-data validation: predicting human label distributions. On ChaosNLI (100 annotations/item), MD-Agreement, and a toxicity dataset with per-annotator labels, build few-shot prompts whose demonstrations include *disagreeing* labels for the same item (or repeated items with different labels) and evaluate the model's predicted label distribution against human distributions (KL, total variation, correlation of entropy). Compare (i) majority-label prompting, (ii) disagreement-revealing prompting, (iii) our probe-conditioned recalibration, and (iv) verbalized-counting CoT. This shows the synthetic deficit predicts a practically important failure and that the fix transfers.
expected_contribution: (1) Bayesian accounts of ICL (Xie et al. 2022; Bayesian scaling laws, Arora et al. 2024; Bayes' Power for Explaining ICL Generalizations, 2025) and PFN/TabPFN work show trained-for-purpose in-context learners approximate posterior predictives, but LLM-side evaluations score *accuracy* or posterior concentration over tasks, never asking whether the model reproduces a *known* conditional label distribution; a Bayesian learner gets aleatoric noise for free, so this is a sharp, previously untested prediction. (2) Noisy-label ICL: Min et al. (2022) randomize labels (maximal noise) and Wei et al. (2023) flip labels, but both report accuracy only; robustness work such as ConDS (2025) treats noise as a nuisance to *filter out* rather than a quantity to *estimate*. (3) LLM calibration (contextual calibration, Zhao et al. 2021; ECE studies) measures confidence vs. correctness, where the ground-truth uncertainty is unknown and confounded with model competence; our synthetic design supplies the exact target distribution, letting us cleanly factor predictive uncertainty into an aleatoric transmission coefficient and an epistemic n-sensitivity term. (4) Distributional-alignment work (ChaosNLI/soft-label prediction, benchmarks of LLM opinion distributions) asks whether models match human label distributions *zero-shot from priors*; we instead ask whether the distribution can be *taught in context*, which is the ICL question and yields a different diagnosis and fix. (5) Mechanistic ICL work (induction heads; task/function vectors; concept encoding-decoding) explains how a single deterministic task label is extracted; nothing there predicts or represents a scalar noise level. We contribute: a stochastic-rule ICL benchmark with exact ground truth, a two-number characterization (beta, epsilon) of ICL uncertainty, evidence that noise rate is encoded-but-unused, a homoscedastic-vs-heteroscedastic dissociation, and a cheap activation-level repair validated on real annotator-disagreement data.
motivation_or_abstract: In-context learning is universally evaluated on deterministic tasks: there is one correct label per input. But most real prediction problems are stochastic, and a competent learner should infer not just the mapping but its noise level. We ask whether LLMs can learn a distribution in context. We build prompts whose demonstrations are drawn from an explicitly noisy rule, P(y=A|x)=p with p known to the experimenter, and compare the model's next-token distribution over label verbalizers with the exact Bayesian posterior predictive. This design yields two interpretable numbers per model: an aleatoric transmission coefficient beta, the slope of model log-odds on true in-context log-odds, and an epistemic sensitivity epsilon, how much predictive entropy shrinks as demonstrations accumulate under a deterministic rule. We predict and test noise blindness: beta far below 1 (predictive distributions collapse toward the majority label, ignoring in-context stochasticity) together with small epsilon (confidence barely tracks evidence quantity), so LLMs' predictive uncertainty is largely decoupled from both components of the ground truth. We further dissociate homoscedastic from heteroscedastic (input-dependent) noise, showing the latter is essentially unlearned. Mechanistically, we train linear probes showing the in-context noise rate *is* linearly decodable from mid-layer activations, i.e. the information is present but not routed to the output; steering along this decoded direction, or an affine logit recalibration conditioned on the decoded rate, recovers most of the gap to the Bayesian oracle at negligible cost. Small transformers meta-trained on stochastic tasks achieve beta near 1, showing the deficit is distributional, not architectural. Finally, on ChaosNLI and other multi-annotator datasets our repair improves prediction of human label distributions over standard few-shot prompting.
problem_statement: Every ICL benchmark assumes a deterministic latent function from x to y, so we do not know whether LLMs can infer a *stochastic* rule in context. We hypothesize an asymmetry we call noise blindness: when demonstrations are generated by a known noisy rule (P(y=A|x)=p), LLMs' predictive distributions transmit only a small fraction of the in-context aleatoric rate (log-odds slope beta << 1, i.e. mode collapse toward the majority label), while simultaneously being nearly insensitive to the epistemic uncertainty that should shrink with the number of demonstrations. Because the noise rate is nonetheless linearly decodable from the residual stream, this is a routing failure that a single training-free steering/recalibration knob can largely repair.
